_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Linda Lou Howarth of Tatla Lake, located west of Williams Lake, couldn’t be more proud of her grandson as she continues to sell homemade breads and buns to be able to watch him compete in Las Vegas at the upcoming YETI Junior National Finals Rodeo (NFR). Tanner Loring, 16, of Riske Creek is one of more than 700 young cowboys and cowgirls who will be heading to the entertainment capital of the world in December after qualifying for novice bull riding. In Williams Lake at the Bewitching Market on Saturday, Oct. 10, Linda could be found with Tanner’s great-aunt Ivy Bowe selling fresh frybread and fry dawgs. Sales that evening went towards paying for Linda and her husband, Loring’s grandfather, flight to Vegas to watch their grandson. “When I heard he was going to Vegas, I just hit every market I could to sell bread, and I’m doing quite well,” Linda said, adding that when her grandson is on television, she’s glued to the screen. In addition to the Bewitching Market, Linda also baked bread and buns to sell at various markets throughout the area over the summer. Bella Coola was where she was most successful with her sales, supporting their travel to Las Vegas. She has raised over $2,000. “We’re quite excited,” Linda said, adding she was able to watch Tanner compete in the B.C. Rodeo Association’s (BCRA) POLARIS Championship Finals Rodeo held at the 77th North Thompson Fall Fair & Rodeo in Barriere. Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

items.title: [downes.ca] When AI Can Make Almost Anything, Judgment Becomes the Job
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Mike Taylor, Mike Taylor | Learning Designer, Speaker & Author, Oct 16, 2026

The argument here, stated about half way through the post, is that "when content becomes abundant, judgment becomes scarce." So "that is where learning professionals can bring more value." Let's think about that. A while ago I proposed a type of AI, called "deontic analytics", would decide what is worthwhile, what is valuable, what should be done. I've seen nothing that suggests AI will be incapable of this. Why would we trust human judgement over AI, if AI can be demonstrably better at this? Consider the new decision models, like Jev and Clef and Decision 1.0 (I'll be a human named that one). It's not obvious that human judgement will always be better. Image: Shadhin.

items.title: [Fast Company] FBI seizes Chinese hacking tools used for cyberattacks on critical U.S. infrastructure
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The FBI has seized scanning and phishing tools used by a group of hackers that officials say is associated with the Chinese government and is believed responsible for disruptive cyber operations in the United States and abroad, including against the power industry, academia and critical infrastructure.

The seizure of the tools, announced Thursday by the FBI and Justice Department, represents the latest law enforcement effort in recent years to go after a broad-based hacking campaign known to the private sector as Flax Typhoon.

The tools at issue, called “Microscan” and “FishHub,” were used by the hackers to scan, phish and hack targets that included U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure, officials said. Microscan was used to target, among other entities, an unnamed power company in the U.S., Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese universities, a multinational, nongovernmental organization and Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies. And “FishHub” facilitated phishing activity that gave hackers remote access to victim networks, the FBI said.

The latest operation has rendered the tools inoperable in what FBI and Justice Department officials said was a blow to the hacking operation.

“We aim to remove the capability from the threat actors. We target their infrastructure, their money, and their tools,” FBI Cyber Division Deputy Assistant Director Jason Bilnoski said in an interview with The Associated Press, calling the hacking operation “indiscriminate and reckless.”

The tools were operated by a Chinese-based information security company called Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI says has contracts with the Chinese government. The company is regarded by the FBI as the true identity of Flax Typhoon.

In Beijing, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China has always cracked down on hacking activities in accordance with the law. Mao said Beijing also firmly opposes spreading disinformation and creating confusion for political purposes, adding that maintaining cybersecurity is a shared concern of both countries.

“We urge the U.S. to abandon its double standards and political manipulation, and work with China through equal dialogue and consultation to jointly address cybersecurity risks,” she said.

In September 2024, the FBI announced that it had disrupted a massive botnet associated with Flax Typhoon that installed malicious software on more than 200,000 consumer devices, including cameras, video recorders and home and office routers, to create a massive botnet. The botnet, or network of infected computers, was used to facilitate cyber crimes, such as the theft of sensitive information from victims’ networks.

FBI San Diego Supervisory Special Agent Brett Lally said that the department would continue to monitor for ways that the company might rebuild its infrastructure.

“It’ll be interesting to see what this round of disruption actions have in terms of their ability to operate as a company in China,” Lally said.

—Safiyah Riddle and Eric Tucker, Associated Press

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover how exercise reverses muscle aging
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a hidden biological mechanism that helps explain how exercise can reverse some of the damage caused by muscle aging. The key is a gene called DEAF1, which becomes overactive with age and interferes with the muscles’ ability to clear damaged proteins and repair themselves. Exercise can help restore this balance, allowing older muscles to rebuild and regain strength, although the benefits may diminish when the system becomes too disrupted.

items.title: [ArchDaily] What Should Exterior Insulation Do Beyond Thermal Performance?
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The buildings and construction sector accounts for around 39% of global CO₂ emissions and nearly 50 per cent of global material extraction. Operational carbon emissions which are associated with the energy consumed to run the buildings also rose by 1% to 9.9 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024, even as building energy use intensity (EUI) has improved. These figures point to persistent gaps in the way buildings are designed, constructed and upgraded. One important area for closing those gaps is the building envelope insulation, which remains central to controlling energy demand, improving thermal resilience and reducing carbon emissions.
